thread.title: Buy These 3 Deeply Undervalued Tech Blue-Chips Before They Soar

author: Dividend Sensei
title: Buy These 3 Deeply Undervalued Tech Blue-Chips Before They Soar
text:
(Source: imgflip )
On Black Friday, a time of bargain hunting for consumers, the S&P 500 ( SPY ) finally closed down 10.2% from its all-time high, officially entering the second correction of the year . However, the Nasdaq ( QQQ ), after enduring its worst monthly performance since 2008 in October, has continued to fall hard and is even potentially threatening a bear market.
^NDX data by YCharts So let's take a look at just why tech stocks, the former darlings of Wall Street, are now so hated. More importantly, find out three reasons why the tech wreck is likely overdone. Thus today is likely a great time to go bargain hunting for attractively priced Grade A tech names, specifically Texas Instruments ( TXN ), Apple ( AAPL ) and Amazon ( AMZN ). Three stocks I'm confident have strong long-term market-beating return potential from today's valuations.
Why Tech Stocks Have Fallen So Hard There are three big reasons that tech stocks have now become so out of favor. The first is simply that, at its October 1st peak the Nasdaq had been on an epic nine-year rally, far outperforming the S&P 500 or the Dow Jones Industrial Index ( DIA ).
QQQ Total Return Price data by YCharts Naturally, such outperformance creates worries among investors that tech stocks are priced for perfection and that severe multiple contraction could occur if any one of the numerous risk factors that make up the ever-present "wall of worry" come true.
There are currently three main risks Wall Street is hyper-focused on. The first is the escalating trade war with China, which is the big reason why the IMF just downgraded its 2018 and 2019 global economic growth forecast yet again (to 3.7% down from 3.9% ). 37% of the S&P 500's revenues come from overseas, meaning that a trade war could represent a painful hit not just to a company's bottom line (due to supply chain disruption) but its top line as well.
(Source: FactSet Research)
No industry is more exposed to a trade war then technology, where 58% of sales come from overseas. This brings us to the second major risk factor that the market is obsessing over, slower earnings growth in 2019.
(Source: FactSet Research)
No one expected 2019's EPS growth to come close to the approximately 20% that we're on track to hit in 2018 (thanks largely to corporate tax cuts). However, 2019 analyst consensus EPS growth estimates have been coming down rapidly, since peaking at 10.4% earlier this year. Part of this is due to falling energy earnings expectations due to the recent oil crash . But while tech firms won't be hurt by low oil prices, a trade war is expected to hit earnings hard.
(Source: FactSet Research )
That's why analyst forecasts for the tech sector's revenue and earnings growth next year is now running slightly below that of the broader market and far below this year's blowout results.
Finally, Wall Street is concerned that slower growth combined with higher interest rates, will mean that tech stock multiples (like PE ratios) are going to contract significantly in the coming year (and possibly beyond).
(Source: FOMC)
That's understandable given that the Fed's latest Dot Plot or long-term guidance about interest rates calls for five or even six more rate hikes. While the Fed's hikes only affect short-term bond yields (like the 2-year) and not long-term rates (like the 10-year) given the flat yield curve higher 2-year yields could still cause some investors to pull money out of riskier tech names in favor of higher "risk-free" returns.
But while all of these risks are real, there are three reasons why I'm still a long-term bull on tech and think that today is likely a great time to go bargain hunting in the sector's most dominant blue-chip names.
3 Reasons Why Today Is Likely A Great Time To Buy Quality Tech Names At A Discount The first reason I'm now a tech bull is the difference between risks and fundamentals. Risks are merely what might go wrong to hurt fundamentals, but fundamentals (sales, earnings, and cash flow) are ultimately what determines the fair value of a stock.
(Source: FactSet Research)
FAANG stocks reported earnings that many on Wall Street saw as disappointing, which was a big reason for the recent sell-off in these former high flyers. However, in reality with rare exceptions (such as NVIDIA) most tech stocks reported excellent results. In fact, 69% beat on their top lines, with 92% reporting better than expected earnings.
(Source: FactSet Research)
What's more, those 92% of tech stocks that beat on earnings did so by an impressive 8%, which was above the overall market's positive surprise rate.
Ok, so maybe tech earnings were good THIS QUARTER. But the market is forward-looking and next year the sector's growth rate is expected to fall off a cliff thanks largely to the trade war. But there's good news on that front as well. On November 2nd President Trump hinted that a China/US trade deal could be coming relatively soon .
“We’ve had a very good discussion with China, we’re getting much closer to doing something ...I spoke with President Xi (Jinping) yesterday. They very much want to make a deal...I think we’ll make a deal with China , and I think it will be a very fair deal for everybody, but it will be a good deal for the United States.” - Donald Trump (emphasis added)
What's more, various sources are reporting that Trump has ordered administration officials to draw up papers to end the trade conflict, indicating that his optimism isn't merely words. Then on November 13th Larry Kudlow, the director of the National Economic Council, told reporters that even lower-level officials were being empowered to hammer out a framework for a final trade deal to be completed .
On November 15th the Financial Times reported that numerous sources say that at the G20 Summit (Nov 30th and Dec 1st):
"they expected Trump and Xi to reach a handshake agreement that would put a pause on the escalation of tensions without actually resolving the underlying issues. It's the same tactic Trump used in negotiations on trade with the European Union and on denuclearization with North Korea ." - Financial Times (emphasis added)
Of course, there is no guarantee of good trade news next week. But as growth in both China's and America's economies has been slowing in recent months (and their stock markets have tumbled) it seems likely that a handshake "deal to make a deal in the future" is indeed likely. That would probably put current tariff escalation plans on hold, which would mean that tech earnings next year would likely come in better than currently expected.
What's more, this positive news is likely just what the market needs to find a bottom, including battered tech blue-chips. Or to put another way, the tech wreck is likely to end relatively soon so buying now is likely to be a great long-term move for investors.
The Market Correction Is Likely Nearly Over And Many Great Tech Stocks Are Now Undervalued Given that tech makes up 23% of the S&P 500 , and is what has driven the broader market into a correction, understanding when tech is likely to bottom is likely to closely correlate with where stocks bottom in general.
While history can only provide a rough estimate of what any given correction is likely to look like, since 1965 the average correction has taken three months to bottom, with stocks falling 12.3% from their all-time highs (including February's correction of -10.2%).
Perhaps more useful for our purposes would be to consider the late 2015 correction, which also lasted about three months, and saw the market drop a total of 13.3% before bottoming. Why focus on that correction? Because the risk factors back then are very similar to what we're facing now:
rising interest rate fears worries over China's slowing economy concerns over slowing global economic growth (and US growth as well) falling oil prices If this correction indeed proves to be similar to the last one, then stocks in general, are likely to fall just 2% to 4% more. Tech stocks might decline 3% to 5% more, due to their naturally higher volatilities (beta above 1).
But why am I confident that tech stocks are likely close to their bottoms rather than setting up for another epic crash like in 2000 to 2003 when the Nasdaq plunged 80% peak to trough? Because today the sector's valuations are already at reasonable levels.
(Source: FactSet Research)
The forward PE on the tech sector is down to 15.6, even accounting for bearish 2019 EPS growth assumptions largely connected to a trade war that is likely to end in the first half of 2019 (or might be put on hold December 1st). That's pretty reasonable given that it bakes in just 3.6% long-term EPS growth, which is already below the consensus forecast (which I believe will prove overly pessimistic).
And if tech stocks do fall another 3% to 5%? Well, then the forward PE for the sector falls to 14.8 to 15.1. Not just is that below the five-year average, but it's in line with the 10-year average which includes the Great Recession when tech stocks fell off a cliff.
Ok, so maybe tech valuations are now much improved and even reasonable, and an end to the trade war might be just the catalyst that causes them (and stocks in general) to bottom and head higher. But that's short-term thinking, and my goal is to always keep investor's attention on the long-term fundamentals (the facts). And the fact is that tech stocks are one of the best sectors to own if you're bullish on the US (and global) economy. And if you're not? Well, why are you investing in stocks at all?
Tech Is One Of The Best Sectors To Own In A Growing Economy And Most Interest Rate Environments Rising long-term interest rates, one of the big fears of today, is usually thought to be a hindrance for tech stocks because higher 10-year yields mean lower PE ratios (in theory). In reality, since 1970 Tech stocks have been the best performing sector when 10-year yields were rising.
That's because long-term rates usually mean rising inflation expectations, due to a strong economy. But wait a second? Isn't the bond market signaling that long-term rates are likely near their peak during this tightening cycle?
Indeed they are, with bond futures predicting just three more Fed rate hikes, which, based on historical data, would indicate that the 10 and 30 year-yields are likely to peak at about 3.35% and 3.5%, respectively. That also implies that the next recession isn't likely to start until late 2020, at the earliest .
But the thing to remember about tech stocks is that they are one of the best sectors to own in every interest rate environment with the exception of a recession, or just before a recession (the so-called "bear steepening yield curve regime").
That's based on date from 1995 to 2017 from BlackRock ( BLK ) the world's largest asset manager. Today we're in a bear flattening yield curve environment (rising rates with short-term rates rising faster than long-term yields). This literally means that today's interest rate environment is the one where tech is most likely to outperform, especially if you buy at low valuations during a bear market for individual tech stocks.
Ok, so maybe the bond market is saying that no recession is coming soon and so tech stocks should go up. But what if the bond market is wrong and we fall into a recession next year as some investors fear? Fortunately, that's not likely based on 19 leading economic indicators that have historically proven to be accurate at predicting the last four recessions.
(Source: Economic PI)
Macroeconomic nerd economic PI (a business owner with a degree in economics, like myself), tracks these leading indicators on a weekly basis and compares them to their historical baseline and rates of change. That comparison can be useful for showing whether each indicator is signaling an expanding or contracting economy.
(Source: Economic PI)
You can then use the mean of coordinates to get an overall idea of the fundamental health of the economy (not necessarily correlated with the growth rate). Today 16 of 19 indicators are pointing to a growing economy.
(Source: Economic PI)
More importantly, the short-term (three months), and long-term (12 months) trends remain positive, with the overall economy remaining healthy and showing little risks of a recession starting anytime soon. That agrees with both BlackStone's ( BX ) Byron Wien ( no recession until 2021 at the earliest ) as well as the 2/10 yield curve.
Back in August the bond market was predicting the Fed would overdo it on rate hikes and soon invert the yield curve (which 90% of the time since 1955 has meant a recession within six to 24 months). But despite the recent correction triggering a flight to safety (falling bond yields), the 2/10 yield curve has remained highly stable over the last few months. That's because slowing economic growth expectations (and easing inflation) have the bond market predicting that a curve inversion is likely far off in the future.
More importantly, the 2/30 yield-curve, which similarly tends to invert about 17 months before the start of a recession, has not just stabilized recently, but been trending higher. Why does that matter? Because according to a 2017 study by the Federal Reserve, QE might have pushed 10-year yields down 85 basis points by 2017 , right before the Fed started rolling off its balance sheet. Accounting for the 10-year treasuries the Fed has allowed to mature without rolling over into new bonds (what the roll off entails) the 10-year yield might still be 70 basis points depressed .
The 30 year-yield was not affected by QE because the Fed never bought 30-year Treasuries. The 2/30 curve has been flattening 6.3 basis points per month since peaking in November 2016. At that rate, it would take another eight months to invert (July 2019) and thus signal a recession would be most likely to begin in early 2021. That would indicate, based on historical averages, that the next bear market (stocks peaking) isn't likely to begin until mid to late 2020 .
But note that even though I remain bullish on both the economy, market, and tech stocks in particular (due to the correction), I am not recommending just blindly buying the sector. Rather three tech stocks, in particular, have found their way into my portfolio during this most recent tech wreck.
3 Grade A Tech Blue-Chips Worth Buying Today These are three tech blue-chips I bought during the recent correction (when each fell into a bear market). They all remain in one today and are at least 14% undervalued and likely to deliver about 15+% long-term CAGR total returns (over the coming decade). Combined they make up 10% of my portfolio.
Texas Instruments ( TXN )
Fair Value Estimate: $131 Discount To Fair Value: 27% Decline From ATH: 20.7% Yield: 3.2% Long-Term EPS Growth (10-year analyst consensus): 11.9% Valuation-adjusted annualized total return (over next decade): 18.2% There are 5 Reasons Why I was buying Texas Instruments so aggressively during this correction . One of those is the company's rich history of innovation, including literally inventing the integrated circuit that underpins today's global economy, as well as decades of profitable R&D that's resulted in over 45,000 patents.
(Source: Texas Instruments Capital Management Update )
More importantly, those patents have been translated into steady growth in free cash flow per share that has made Texas Instruments a dividend growth dream stock (36 fold increase in the payout since 2004). That's courtesy of the disciplined management team returning 100% of free cash flow to shareholders in the form of dividends and buybacks.
Today the company's long-term growth runway remains strong, courtesy of its focus on industrial and automotive sectors, which will be helped immensely by the rise of 5G and the internet of things. Analysts expect about 12% long-term EPS and FCF/share growth, which is in line with its historical norm.
Over the past 13 years, Texas Instruments' yield has been stable around 2.35%, including numerous industry downturns and even the Great Recession. Under Dividend Yield Theory (see the watchlist section of my portfolio updates for an in-depth guide to this time-tested dividend stock valuation method ) that implies TXN is about 27% undervalued. That means that over the next decade, the stock's return to fair value (on an annualized basis) when combined with its dividend yield and long-term EPS/FCF/dividend growth rate, should generate about 18% total returns.
Amazon ( AMZN )
Fair Value Estimate: $2,200 Discount To Fair Value: 32% Decline From ATH: 26.4% Yield: 0% Long-Term EPS Growth (10-year analyst consensus): 47.3% Valuation-adjusted annualized total return (over next decade): 18.9% to 23.9% Amazon is currently the only non-dividend stock I own and by far one of the hardest growth stocks to value. For my fair value estimate, I use Morningstar's three-stage discounted free cash flow model using the following assumptions.
Morningstar's Joe Gemino Amazon Sales Growth Assumptions (through 2022)
physical stores: 9% CAGR online retail: 10% CAGR third-party seller services: 25% CAGR AWS: 33% (with operating margins rising to 30%, already surpassed) Subscription Services (Prime): 37% CAGR Advertising: 66% CAGR Overall company sales growth: 22% CAGR Overall operating margins: 8% to 9% (vs. 6.6% in Q3 2018) Overall company operating income growth: 38% CAGR I personally believe these to be reasonable, given the massive growth drivers enjoyed by the company. That's why I tripled my position in Amazon during the stock's most recent bear market . The stock has been slammed due to fears that 10% to 20% Q4 revenue guidance means the company's strong growth days are over.
However, FactSet is estimating that in Q4 (the holiday quarter) Amazon's stupendous earnings growth will account for 50% of all EPS growth in the entire retail industry . That's because according to Adobe Analytics, online sales (on Black Friday) are tracking for a 29% increase over last year and the analyst firm is forecasting 17% overall e-commerce sales growth this holiday season. That bodes well for Amazon hitting the upper end of its top-line growth guidance, which is firmly within its historical norm over the previous decade.
AMZN Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts
Factor in the fact that earnings are likely to continue rapidly outpacing sales due to the fast growth rates of high margin AWS (30% operating margin) and advertising (75% operating margin), and I have no qualms about recommending Amazon at today's prices. In fact, despite the certainty that long-term EPS and cash flow growth will slow (due to the law of large numbers) I still expect shares bought today to generate at least about 19% CAGR total returns over the coming years.
Apple ( AAPL )
Fair Value Estimate: $200 Discount To Fair Value: 14% Decline From ATH: 25.8% Yield: 1.7% Long-Term EPS Growth (10-year analyst consensus): 13.1% Valuation-adjusted annualized total return (over next decade): 14.8% to 16.3% Apple's latest bear market was, as in the past, triggered by rampant speculation that peak iPhone will doom the company. However, there are four things investors need to know about Apple's plunge into a bear market . The most important is that, despite long-term sales growth forecasts of just mid-single digits, driven by the company's massive and fast-growing subscription service base, Apple's bottom line is expected to keep growing at double digits for the foreseeable future.
(Source: Motley Fool )

In fact, Apple's long-term growth rate is expected to keep up with that of the last five years, when the shares have returned 154% (20.5% CAGR returns), even factoring in the recent crash.
That strong bottom line growth (ultimately what drives the share price) is going to come a lot from Apple's epic buyback program in which management still have $123 billion of dry powder to deploy.
(Source: Apple)
That's because Apple has said it wants to get to a net cash (cash minus debt) position of zero eventually. In the past 12 months, Apple generated $64 billion in free cash flow, $50 billion of which was added to the balance sheet after paying its rapidly growing dividend. Even when Apple's excess cash pile is gone, the company will still be one of the strongest repurchasers of its shares, which should help drive about 13% EPS/FCF/dividend growth for many years to come.
Combined with shares that are about 14% undervalued today (12.8 times forward earnings), that should allow Apple to deliver 15% to 16% long-term total returns. For a low risk blue-chip of this caliber, that's strong enough to not just recommend you buy it, but take an initial stake in the company myself. I've also set limits at lower levels, to lock in additional undervalued shares in case the market wants to offer me this Grade A blue-chip at an even better bargain.
Bottom Line: Now Is A Great Time To Go Bargain Hunting For Quality Tech Names Readers have asked me why my portfolio is so heavily weighted in energy, utilities, REITs and pharma, and until recently, no tech. That's because I'm a contrarian value investor who puts my capital to work into the most undervalued quality dividend growth opportunities I can find. That means waiting until a sector becomes hated for short-term reasons that don't harm a company's strong underlying fundamentals and long-term growth thesis.
Tech is a sector that even Warren Buffett has said value investors need to focus more heavily on in the coming decades . I 100% agree with that assessment but also that one should "be greedy when others are fearful". That means waiting for market sentiment, which is fickle, to turn against tech before buying the top quality names that best suits your portfolio's long-term goals.
And when Wall Street runs deep red with the shattered dreams of momentum traders? Well, that's when highly volatile tech stocks like Texas Instruments, Apple, and Amazon can crash fast and hard. But for smart long-term value investors, such volatility isn't a bug, it's a feature. One that we embrace as we would a lover because it allows us to buy even Grade A tech stocks at deep discounts to fair value. Never forget that, with stocks in general, but tech in particular, bull markets make you money, but in the long-term, bear markets make you rich.
Disclosure: I am/we are long BLK, TXN, AMZN, AAPL.
